parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 14. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman asking about voluntary work at a community centre. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 7. Graham: Good morning, Hatfield Community Centre. Graham speaking. Chloe: Oh, hello. My name's Chloe Watts. I saw a poster in the post office saying that you're looking for volunteers. Graham: Yes, we certainly are. Thank you for calling. Have you done any voluntary work before? Chloe: Not for a while. I helped out at a youth club when I was at university, but I've only just moved to Hatfield, and I'd like to get involved in something local. I work from home three days a week, so I've got a bit of time. Graham: That's great. Well, there are quite a few things you could help with. One is our toy library. Families can borrow toys for a few weeks, and then bring them back and choose some more. It's very popular. Chloe: What sort of help do you need there? Graham: Well, sorting them out on the shelves is fairly quick. The main job is cleaning the toys when they come back, before they go out again. With small children, that's really important. Chloe: Yes, I can imagine. Graham: We also need someone to look after the list of loans, so we know who's got what. We used to use a card index, but now it's all on a spreadsheet, and to be honest, it's got a bit out of date. Are you OK with computers? Chloe: Yes, that's fine. I use spreadsheets all the time at work. Graham: Perfect. The toy library's open on Saturday mornings, in the Willow Room. That's the one at the back of the building, next to the kitchen. Chloe: OK. Willow, like the tree? Graham: That's right. All the rooms here are named after trees. The main hall used to be called the Oak Room, but nobody ever used that name. Chloe: What else is there? Graham: Well, there's the homework club, which runs on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons for children from the local primary school. Most of the volunteers there help with reading, but what we're really short of is people who can help the children with maths. A lot of parents feel they can't do it themselves, because the methods have changed so much. Chloe: I studied economics, so I'd be happy to do that. Graham: Excellent. Because you'd be working with children, you'd need to have a background check before you start. It's quite straightforward, and we pay for it, but it can take a few weeks. Chloe: That's fine. Graham: And then there are one or two people who need help at the moment. Next Wednesday, for example, Mr Okoro needs someone to take him to the dentist. He used to go to the health centre in the village, but he's had to change to a surgery in town, and he doesn't drive. Chloe: I could do that. I've got a car. Graham: Oh, that would be great. And Mrs Fenton has just come out of hospital after an operation on her knee, and she needs someone to do her shopping for the next couple of weeks. Her daughter usually does it, but she's away. Chloe: I could do that. There's a supermarket just round the corner from me. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 8 to 10. Graham: We also have a few special events coming up, and we always need extra help for those. Chloe: What sort of events? Graham: Well, on the fourteenth of October, we're holding an auction in the main hall to raise money for a new roof. Local businesses have donated all sorts of things, from meals in restaurants to a weekend in a holiday cottage. Chloe: What would I need to do for that? Graham: We've already got people to set up the room and serve the refreshments, but we need someone to take photos during the evening, for the website. Chloe: Oh, I'm not bad at that. I've got quite a good camera. Graham: Great. Then on the fifth of November there's the bonfire night party on the sports field. There'll be fireworks, of course, and we're selling food to raise money. Someone's already offered to run the barbecue, but we need people to sell soup. It's usually freezing, so it's very popular. Chloe: I'd enjoy that. And is there anything at Christmas? Graham: Yes, the carol concert. That's on the twentieth of December, and this year it'll be in St Mark's Church, because the hall's too small. We'll need help making decorations for the church. The children from the homework club will be helping too. Chloe: That sounds fun. What about tickets? Do people have to buy them in advance? Graham: No, it's free, although we do ask for donations at the door. Chloe: OK. Well, I'd like to help with as many things as I can. What should I do next? Graham: If you could come in and fill in a form, I can show you around at the same time. Are you free on Friday morning? Chloe: Yes, that's fine. Is there anywhere to park? Graham: There's a small car park behind the building, but it fills up quickly, so it's often easier to park in the street. Oh, and we have a volunteers' lunch on the last Friday of every month, so you'll get a chance to meet everyone. Chloe: That sounds lovely. Thanks very much, Graham. I'll see you on Friday. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a guide at a nature reserve called Marsh End talking to a group of visitors. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Marsh End Nature Reserve. My name's Tom, and I'm one of the wardens here. Before you set off, I'd like to tell you a little about the reserve and what you can do here. Many visitors assume that this has always been natural wetland, but in fact, fifty years ago, this whole area was a gravel quarry. When the digging stopped, the pits filled with water, and a local wildlife trust bought the land and turned it into the reserve you see today. There was a serious flood here in the nineteen nineties, which actually helped by creating some new areas of reed bed. Guide: Now, we do some research here, and we run a lot of school visits, but our main purpose is to protect the bittern. It's a shy brown bird, a member of the heron family, and it had almost disappeared from this country. We now have six breeding pairs, which is one of the largest populations in the region. Every spring, the wardens count the booming males to work out how many birds there are. You'll be very lucky to see one, as they're extremely well camouflaged, but you might hear the males calling. It's a deep booming sound, a bit like someone blowing across the top of a bottle. Guide: If you want to know more about the birds you've seen, we don't have leaflets any more, I'm afraid, and there's no app for the reserve yet. But the best thing to do is to ask one of our volunteers. There's usually at least one in each of the hides, and they know a huge amount. Guide: We've made a few changes this year. The bird-feeding station by the car park has been there for years, and we've had a children's trail for a while too. What's new is the floating walkway across the main lake, which opened in April. It moves slightly as you walk on it, which children love, and it takes you right into the middle of the reed beds. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Guide: Let me tell you about the different areas of the reserve. We're standing in the visitor centre at the moment. Upstairs, there's a café with a lovely view over the water, and it serves hot meals as well as drinks and cakes, so it's a good place to come back to for lunch. The toilets and baby-changing facilities are also here. We used to hire out binoculars from the desk down here, but so many were never returned that we've had to stop, I'm afraid. Guide: From here, the path leads to the Lake Hide. This is where most visitors spend their time, and it's the best place on the reserve for watching birds, especially ducks and geese in the winter. People sometimes bring bread to feed the ducks, but please don't, as it's very bad for them. Guide: Beyond the Lake Hide is the pond-dipping platform. Here you can use a net to catch water creatures like beetles, snails and dragonfly larvae, and there are trays and magnifying glasses so you can look at them closely before you put them back. It's very popular with children, but adults enjoy it just as much. Guide: Further along the lake is the Old Boathouse. It's no longer used for boats, but it's where we have our shop, selling books, cards and gifts made by local craftspeople. All the money goes towards the work of the reserve. Guide: Next to the boathouse is the jetty. From there, you can go out on the lake in our electric boat, with one of the wardens as your guide. Trips leave every hour, and you can book your place at the jetty itself. Each trip lasts about forty minutes, and children under twelve must wear a life jacket, which we provide. Guide: And finally, there's the wildflower meadow, on the far side of the reserve. It's not very large, but it's home to several rare plants, including three kinds of wild orchid, which are flowering at the moment. Please keep to the paths there, as the plants are very easily damaged. Right, has anyone got any questions before you set off? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two music students, Lucy and Sam, discussing a production of Mozart's opera The Magic Flute. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 and 22. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 and 22. Lucy: So, Sam, we need to start planning our review of The Magic Flute. Have you looked at the guidelines? Sam: Yes. I was going to start with a bit about the history of the opera, when Mozart wrote it and so on. Lucy: I don't think that's necessary. Our tutor said everyone knows that already, and it just wastes words. And we don't need anything about Mozart's life either. We did that last term. Sam: Fair enough. What about a summary of the story? Lucy: Only a sentence or two. The guidelines say they want to know what we actually felt about the performance. It's supposed to be our own response, not an essay. Sam: Right. And I think we should pick out two or three particular scenes and describe them in detail. That makes it much more vivid. Lucy: Definitely. The Queen of the Night's second aria, for a start. Sam: OK. And how long does it need to be? Lucy: About fifteen hundred words, so we'll have to be quite selective. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 23 to 27. Now listen and answer questions 23 to 27. Sam: So, what did you think of the set? Lucy: I thought it was brilliant. That huge revolving staircase in the middle of the stage, which turned into a forest, then a temple, then a prison. Sam: Me too. It was easily the best thing about the whole production. I've never seen anything like it. Lucy: And the lighting worked really well with it. When the stage went almost dark in the trial scenes, with just a few candles, it really did feel mysterious and a bit frightening. Sam: Yes, it was exactly right for those scenes. What about the costumes? I was surprised they were so modern. Papageno in a tracksuit. Lucy: So was I. From the posters, I'd assumed they would be using the kind of costumes you'd have seen in Mozart's day, wigs and long coats and so on. I didn't mind the modern ones, though. Sam: No, neither did I, once I got used to them. But the orchestra was a let-down, wasn't it? Lucy: It was. It was the thing I was most looking forward to, and they just sounded tired. Some of the fast passages were quite messy. Sam: I agree. It was a real shame. And what about the singers' acting? Some of them hardly moved. Lucy: I think that was the director's fault. He seemed to want them to stand still and just sing. Sam: Really? I thought it was more that some of them are just not very good actors. They're trained as singers, after all, not actors. Lucy: Hmm. Well, we can mention both points of view in the review. Our tutor always says a good review should be balanced anyway. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 28 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 28 to 30. Sam: The guidelines also ask us to say whether the opera is a good choice for young audiences. There were lots of teenagers there. Lucy: I think it's ideal, though not because of its length. It's nearly three hours with the interval. And I'm not sure the moral lessons about wisdom and virtue mean much to teenagers. Sam: No. But it's got a fairy-tale story, with a dragon and magic instruments, and at the same time there's lots of comedy, especially from Papageno. That mixture seems to appeal to young people. Lucy: Yes, the teenagers behind us were laughing all the way through. And the fact that it was sung in English must have helped too. Sam: I wasn't sure about that at first. I thought it might be distracting, as I know the German words quite well. Lucy: I felt the same, but actually I found it made the story much easier to follow. I didn't have to keep looking up at the surtitles. Sam: Yes, that's true. I didn't expect that, but I ended up enjoying it more. Lucy: Finally, the guidelines ask why we think Mozart's operas are performed all over the world. What do you think? Sam: Well, people often say it's the tunes, and they are very catchy. And the characters are memorable. Lucy: True, but lots of composers have good tunes. I think the real reason is that you can enjoy the music even if you don't understand a word of the story. The music expresses everything the characters are feeling. Sam: That's a good point. Audiences in Tokyo or Buenos Aires don't need to speak German to be moved by it. Let's make that our conclusion. I'll write a first draft of the introduction this weekend, and you could do the section on the set and the lighting. Lucy: OK. Send me your draft when it's ready, and I'll have my section done by Monday. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer on a linguistics course talking about the Welsh language. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: In today's lecture, I'm going to look at Welsh, the Celtic language spoken in Wales, and at the efforts that have been made to keep it alive. Welsh is one of the oldest languages in Europe still in everyday use, and some of the earliest poetry written in it dates back around fourteen hundred years. Yet, like many minority languages, it has come under enormous pressure from a much larger neighbour. I'll look first at the situation today, then at the history of the language, and finally at what is being done to support it. Lecturer: According to the most recent census, carried out in twenty twenty-one, about eighteen per cent of people in Wales can speak Welsh. That's around half a million people. It may not sound very many, but the Welsh government has set itself an ambitious target: it wants the number of Welsh speakers to reach one million by the year twenty fifty. The figure varies enormously, though. In some areas of the north-west, it is well over half the population. Lecturer: To understand why the language needs this kind of support, we need to look at its history. In the fifteen thirties, laws uniting Wales with England made English the language of the law courts, and anyone who used Welsh could not hold public office. For centuries afterwards, many parents believed that English was the key to a better job for their children. In the nineteenth century, many schools tried to stop children speaking Welsh in the classroom. A child who was heard speaking Welsh might be made to wear a piece of wood hung round their neck, with the letters W N carved on it, standing for Welsh Not. The child wearing it at the end of the day was often punished. Historians still debate how widely it was used, but it has become a powerful symbol of the pressure the language was under. Lecturer: By the middle of the twentieth century, the number of speakers was falling fast. A turning point came in nineteen sixty-two, when the writer Saunders Lewis gave a radio lecture in which he warned that Welsh would die out by the end of the century unless people took action. The lecture was called, in English, The Fate of the Language. His words inspired a new generation of campaigners, who painted over English-only road signs and demanded that Welsh be given equal status. One of their greatest successes came in nineteen eighty-two, when a Welsh-language television channel was launched, after one senior politician threatened to go on hunger strike. The channel still broadcasts today, and it has produced several drama series that have been sold around the world. Lecturer: Education has been central to the revival. Since nineteen ninety-nine, all pupils in Wales have had to study Welsh until the age of sixteen. And Welsh-medium schools, where most subjects are taught through Welsh, have become increasingly popular, including with parents who don't speak the language themselves. Many of them want their children to have the advantages of being bilingual. Research suggests that children who grow up with two languages may also find it easier to learn a third. Lecturer: Adults are learning too. Evening classes have existed for decades, but online courses have made a huge difference. They became particularly popular during the lockdown in twenty twenty, when many people suddenly had time on their hands, and some language apps reported that Welsh was one of their fastest-growing languages in Britain. The government has also funded a national centre for learning Welsh, which organises courses for adults across the country. Lecturer: However, there are still serious challenges. In some rural and coastal areas, where Welsh has traditionally been strongest, many houses are now bought as second homes, which are empty for much of the year. Young local people often can't afford to buy property, and they move away, taking the language with them. On the other hand, the number of speakers in the capital, Cardiff, has been rising, largely because of Welsh-medium education. Another problem is that many young people who learn Welsh at school stop using it once they leave school, because they have few opportunities to speak it at work or in their social lives. So the challenge now is not just to teach Welsh, but to make sure that people actually use it in their daily lives. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a guide at a nature reserve called Marsh End talking to a group of visitors. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Marsh End Nature Reserve. My name's Tom, and I'm one of the wardens here. Before you set off, I'd like to tell you a little about the reserve and what you can do here. Many visitors assume that this has always been natural wetland, but in fact, fifty years ago, this whole area was a gravel quarry. When the digging stopped, the pits filled with water, and a local wildlife trust bought the land and turned it into the reserve you see today. There was a serious flood here in the nineteen nineties, which actually helped by creating some new areas of reed bed. Guide: Now, we do some research here, and we run a lot of school visits, but our main purpose is to protect the bittern. It's a shy brown bird, a member of the heron family, and it had almost disappeared from this country. We now have six breeding pairs, which is one of the largest populations in the region. Every spring, the wardens count the booming males to work out how many birds there are. You'll be very lucky to see one, as they're extremely well camouflaged, but you might hear the males calling. It's a deep booming sound, a bit like someone blowing across the top of a bottle. Guide: If you want to know more about the birds you've seen, we don't have leaflets any more, I'm afraid, and there's no app for the reserve yet. But the best thing to do is to ask one of our volunteers. There's usually at least one in each of the hides, and they know a huge amount. Guide: We've made a few changes this year. The bird-feeding station by the car park has been there for years, and we've had a children's trail for a while too. What's new is the floating walkway across the main lake, which opened in April. It moves slightly as you walk on it, which children love, and it takes you right into the middle of the reed beds. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Guide: Let me tell you about the different areas of the reserve. We're standing in the visitor centre at the moment. Upstairs, there's a café with a lovely view over the water, and it serves hot meals as well as drinks and cakes, so it's a good place to come back to for lunch. The toilets and baby-changing facilities are also here. We used to hire out binoculars from the desk down here, but so many were never returned that we've had to stop, I'm afraid. Guide: From here, the path leads to the Lake Hide. This is where most visitors spend their time, and it's the best place on the reserve for watching birds, especially ducks and geese in the winter. People sometimes bring bread to feed the ducks, but please don't, as it's very bad for them. Guide: Beyond the Lake Hide is the pond-dipping platform. Here you can use a net to catch water creatures like beetles, snails and dragonfly larvae, and there are trays and magnifying glasses so you can look at them closely before you put them back. It's very popular with children, but adults enjoy it just as much. Guide: Further along the lake is the Old Boathouse. It's no longer used for boats, but it's where we have our shop, selling books, cards and gifts made by local craftspeople. All the money goes towards the work of the reserve. Guide: Next to the boathouse is the jetty. From there, you can go out on the lake in our electric boat, with one of the wardens as your guide. Trips leave every hour, and you can book your place at the jetty itself. Each trip lasts about forty minutes, and children under twelve must wear a life jacket, which we provide. Guide: And finally, there's the wildflower meadow, on the far side of the reserve. It's not very large, but it's home to several rare plants, including three kinds of wild orchid, which are flowering at the moment. Please keep to the paths there, as the plants are very easily damaged. Right, has anyone got any questions before you set off? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two music students, Lucy and Sam, discussing a production of Mozart's opera The Magic Flute. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 and 22. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 and 22. Lucy: So, Sam, we need to start planning our review of The Magic Flute. Have you looked at the guidelines? Sam: Yes. I was going to start with a bit about the history of the opera, when Mozart wrote it and so on. Lucy: I don't think that's necessary. Our tutor said everyone knows that already, and it just wastes words. And we don't need anything about Mozart's life either. We did that last term. Sam: Fair enough. What about a summary of the story? Lucy: Only a sentence or two. The guidelines say they want to know what we actually felt about the performance. It's supposed to be our own response, not an essay. Sam: Right. And I think we should pick out two or three particular scenes and describe them in detail. That makes it much more vivid. Lucy: Definitely. The Queen of the Night's second aria, for a start. Sam: OK. And how long does it need to be? Lucy: About fifteen hundred words, so we'll have to be quite selective. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 23 to 27. Now listen and answer questions 23 to 27. Sam: So, what did you think of the set? Lucy: I thought it was brilliant. That huge revolving staircase in the middle of the stage, which turned into a forest, then a temple, then a prison. Sam: Me too. It was easily the best thing about the whole production. I've never seen anything like it. Lucy: And the lighting worked really well with it. When the stage went almost dark in the trial scenes, with just a few candles, it really did feel mysterious and a bit frightening. Sam: Yes, it was exactly right for those scenes. What about the costumes? I was surprised they were so modern. Papageno in a tracksuit. Lucy: So was I. From the posters, I'd assumed they would be using the kind of costumes you'd have seen in Mozart's day, wigs and long coats and so on. I didn't mind the modern ones, though. Sam: No, neither did I, once I got used to them. But the orchestra was a let-down, wasn't it? Lucy: It was. It was the thing I was most looking forward to, and they just sounded tired. Some of the fast passages were quite messy. Sam: I agree. It was a real shame. And what about the singers' acting? Some of them hardly moved. Lucy: I think that was the director's fault. He seemed to want them to stand still and just sing. Sam: Really? I thought it was more that some of them are just not very good actors. They're trained as singers, after all, not actors. Lucy: Hmm. Well, we can mention both points of view in the review. Our tutor always says a good review should be balanced anyway. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 28 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 28 to 30. Sam: The guidelines also ask us to say whether the opera is a good choice for young audiences. There were lots of teenagers there. Lucy: I think it's ideal, though not because of its length. It's nearly three hours with the interval. And I'm not sure the moral lessons about wisdom and virtue mean much to teenagers. Sam: No. But it's got a fairy-tale story, with a dragon and magic instruments, and at the same time there's lots of comedy, especially from Papageno. That mixture seems to appeal to young people. Lucy: Yes, the teenagers behind us were laughing all the way through. And the fact that it was sung in English must have helped too. Sam: I wasn't sure about that at first. I thought it might be distracting, as I know the German words quite well. Lucy: I felt the same, but actually I found it made the story much easier to follow. I didn't have to keep looking up at the surtitles. Sam: Yes, that's true. I didn't expect that, but I ended up enjoying it more. Lucy: Finally, the guidelines ask why we think Mozart's operas are performed all over the world. What do you think? Sam: Well, people often say it's the tunes, and they are very catchy. And the characters are memorable. Lucy: True, but lots of composers have good tunes. I think the real reason is that you can enjoy the music even if you don't understand a word of the story. The music expresses everything the characters are feeling. Sam: That's a good point. Audiences in Tokyo or Buenos Aires don't need to speak German to be moved by it. Let's make that our conclusion. I'll write a first draft of the introduction this weekend, and you could do the section on the set and the lighting. Lucy: OK. Send me your draft when it's ready, and I'll have my section done by Monday. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer on a linguistics course talking about the Welsh language. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: In today's lecture, I'm going to look at Welsh, the Celtic language spoken in Wales, and at the efforts that have been made to keep it alive. Welsh is one of the oldest languages in Europe still in everyday use, and some of the earliest poetry written in it dates back around fourteen hundred years. Yet, like many minority languages, it has come under enormous pressure from a much larger neighbour. I'll look first at the situation today, then at the history of the language, and finally at what is being done to support it. Lecturer: According to the most recent census, carried out in twenty twenty-one, about eighteen per cent of people in Wales can speak Welsh. That's around half a million people. It may not sound very many, but the Welsh government has set itself an ambitious target: it wants the number of Welsh speakers to reach one million by the year twenty fifty. The figure varies enormously, though. In some areas of the north-west, it is well over half the population. Lecturer: To understand why the language needs this kind of support, we need to look at its history. In the fifteen thirties, laws uniting Wales with England made English the language of the law courts, and anyone who used Welsh could not hold public office. For centuries afterwards, many parents believed that English was the key to a better job for their children. In the nineteenth century, many schools tried to stop children speaking Welsh in the classroom. A child who was heard speaking Welsh might be made to wear a piece of wood hung round their neck, with the letters W N carved on it, standing for Welsh Not. The child wearing it at the end of the day was often punished. Historians still debate how widely it was used, but it has become a powerful symbol of the pressure the language was under. Lecturer: By the middle of the twentieth century, the number of speakers was falling fast. A turning point came in nineteen sixty-two, when the writer Saunders Lewis gave a radio lecture in which he warned that Welsh would die out by the end of the century unless people took action. The lecture was called, in English, The Fate of the Language. His words inspired a new generation of campaigners, who painted over English-only road signs and demanded that Welsh be given equal status. One of their greatest successes came in nineteen eighty-two, when a Welsh-language television channel was launched, after one senior politician threatened to go on hunger strike. The channel still broadcasts today, and it has produced several drama series that have been sold around the world. Lecturer: Education has been central to the revival. Since nineteen ninety-nine, all pupils in Wales have had to study Welsh until the age of sixteen. And Welsh-medium schools, where most subjects are taught through Welsh, have become increasingly popular, including with parents who don't speak the language themselves. Many of them want their children to have the advantages of being bilingual. Research suggests that children who grow up with two languages may also find it easier to learn a third. Lecturer: Adults are learning too. Evening classes have existed for decades, but online courses have made a huge difference. They became particularly popular during the lockdown in twenty twenty, when many people suddenly had time on their hands, and some language apps reported that Welsh was one of their fastest-growing languages in Britain. The government has also funded a national centre for learning Welsh, which organises courses for adults across the country. Lecturer: However, there are still serious challenges. In some rural and coastal areas, where Welsh has traditionally been strongest, many houses are now bought as second homes, which are empty for much of the year. Young local people often can't afford to buy property, and they move away, taking the language with them. On the other hand, the number of speakers in the capital, Cardiff, has been rising, largely because of Welsh-medium education. Another problem is that many young people who learn Welsh at school stop using it once they leave school, because they have few opportunities to speak it at work or in their social lives. So the challenge now is not just to teach Welsh, but to make sure that people actually use it in their daily lives. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
